rows.l: - For Sheet-Level Manipulation questions, modify or fill in values ONLY within the cell range given in answer_position — never touch cells outside that range.
- Prefer computing and writing LITERAL values (e.g. with pandas/openpyxl) over live spreadsheet formulas, so the result is unambiguous when the file is re-opened for grading.

+- The grader compares each written cell's TYPE as well as its value, so a whole number stored as the float `25.0` fails a cell that expects the integer `25`, and the text `"5"` fails a cell that expects the number `5`. Enforce the type in code:

+  - To copy an unchanged value, read and write it with openpyxl (`dst_ws[addr] = src_ws[addr].value`) — do NOT route it through pandas/`DataFrame`, which coerces every number to float and every blank to `NaN`.
+  - Before writing a computed number, collapse an integral float to `int`: `v = int(v) if isinstance(v, float) and v.is_integer() else v`.
+  - Keep a value as a float only when it genuinely has a fractional part, and never write a number as a string (or a string as a number).

- When your answer aggregates or transforms a block of SOURCE data whose length can vary (e.g. summing a column, matching or iterating rows until the data ends, copying a variable number of rows), detect the real data extent from the file at run time — scan to the last non-empty row/column, or use openpyxl `ws.max_row` / `ws.max_column` — instead of assuming the row/column count shown in the small preview. This task is graded on other copies of the workbook whose data extent differs from the preview, so code that hard-codes a row count taken from the example will read too few or too many rows on those copies. This affects only how you READ and aggregate the source; the cells you WRITE are still exactly those named in answer_position.
- Always save your result to the exact output_path given, creating any missing parent directories first.
